utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-06-90-T, the Prosecutor versus Ante Gotovina et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Waespi, there was a procedural issue you'd like to raise?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to you Mr. Ryan Carrier, who is a new member of the Prosecution team, and he'd like to address you on the next witness, AG-58. And for that, I think we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Any other procedural matter to be raised? Yes, Mr. Carrier.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. If I could be excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CARRIER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The only outstanding issue I think we had yesterday was the video/audio clips that the Prosecution was going to look at that we had moved to admit into evidence, and there was to be a report back rather quickly. I don't know if it was yesterday or this morning, but they were the two audio clips that were played with Ambassador Galbraith, as you mentioned, a year ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At the time, I think the main objection was that it was not introduced in relation to any testimony by a witness. That might have changed meanwhile, Mr. Waespi?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I have relayed it to Mr. Tieger yesterday, and unfortunately I haven't heard back from him, so I'll make a promise that we'll get it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't think that is such an urgency that we could not allow to you come back to it later today.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: You noted, Mr. President, that it was not in relation to the testimony of any witness. It was, in fact, used during the testimony of Ambassador Galbraith who was present during these discussions on the audiotapes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- and we are talking about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we don't have those numbers. Is it D1451 or --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, let me just -- oh, yes, audio, yes. Let me just have a look. If you give me one second to read it. Yes: "It was not yet MFI'd, and we would hear from you, Mr. Tieger." That's clear. It goes back to the 24th of June. I think I made a nasty remark about one year. That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The comment was that, just so that counsel understands it, it's at 5065, line 22, so if you want to go back and take a look at Mr. Tieger on that, I think that might assist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll then hear from you after approximately one year and two days, instead of one day. We'll hear from you. Any other matter to be raised? If not, Madam Usher, could you please escort the witness into the courtroom. Mr. Waespi, I hardly dare to ask you whether you're ready to cross-examine the witness, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I am, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would also like to hear later today on the completeness of the transcript of P448. There was an issue about whether the transcript was complete or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Zuzul. I would like to remind you that the solemn declaration that you gave yesterday still binds you; that is, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. You'll now be further cross-examined by Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ambassador.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to cover four areas with you this morning. I don't think it should take that long: Let's start with the first one. I'm not sure I -- I'm not sure I fully understood you yesterday, your testimony, about the crimes or events, as you call them, occurring, and your contacts with internationals. That's at page 18327, and I quote from your testimony yesterday: "Since I primarily communicated with the international community, I can say, to the best of my recollection, that in the immediate aftermath of Operation Storm, I never learned that the international community or anyone else should have information to the effect that these events took place on a massive scale. Quite to the contrary." And then you go on to mention Ambassador Galbraith. Now, first of all, when you talk about events, what are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to define precisely what these events were. What I referred to yesterday, speaking from my memory, and what I would repeat today as well, in my contacts with the international community, I really do not remember that any specific concern was raised in respect of some events that would be considered unacceptable by the international community and which would have happened immediately following Storm, such as inadequate protection of the civilian population, burning homes and looting, everything else that was referred to in the later accounts. I have to draw your attention to the fact that we started receiving opinions and reflections from the international community only several weeks later. I wouldn't be able to tell you when, exactly, but this is how I remember it. When I said "our concerns," I meant to say that we had always had in mind the fact that the strategic goal of Croatia was to become part of the international community and that we did care about what sort of a reaction the international community would have to a specific situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But you personally, and you were an ambassador in various capacities at the relevant time, a special envoy of President Tudjman, have you never read any of the numerous documents and, indeed, observations from international sources, United Nations, UNHCR, stating that these events, these crimes in the aftermath of Operation Storm, did take place on a massive scale?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I did not say that I did not read the reports and that I did not hear of them. What I said yesterday, and repeat it today, was, to the best of my recollection, and I might be mistaken because of the lapse of time, such reactions from the international community started coming in several weeks following Storm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you do accept that the international community expressed huge concerns about the burning and looting and that it did happen on a massive scale? Do you accept that today, as you testify now?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am testifying to the truth that I know and the way I know about it. I cannot use your terms of "massive" or "many." This is not how I experienced the contacts with the international community. However, I am aware of such things happening following Operation Storm and perhaps in the aftermath of other operations. It was my impression at the time that these events were not massive, but I did not have an insight into the situation. It was my firm conviction at the time, and I can take the liberty of saying it here, that I never believed that it was part of a systematic plan. These were un-wished-for events that followed the developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at just one example of a document you might have read at the time or seen. D690, this is a statement by the head of UNHCR, Ms. Ogata [Realtime transcript read in error "Rogata"]. Do you remember her?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I knew Madam Ogata.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And she signed or authored that statement on 10th of October, 1995, and on page 1 --

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] By the way, there is a wrong spelling of Madam -- it's not Madam Ogata, but Madam Ogata.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, thank you. The transcript will be reviewed after this court hearing so as to correct any spelling mistakes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you actually meet Ms. Ogata at the time she was in the Balkans in the aftermath of Operation Storm?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether I met with her in the aftermath of Operation Storm, but I did meet with her on several occasions. Her headquarters was in Geneva, and I visited her there on several occasions, and we had generally good cooperation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at this document, and if we can scroll down to the bottom of the document. There, Ms. Ogata addresses this, quote, "serious aggravation of the problem of ethnic intolerance and persecution in recent days," and then she goes on to say that she was, quote, "particularly appalled by the widespread violations of human rights that have been taking place in the Krajina region since it was recaptured by the Croatian Army in August. Burning and looting of Serb homes have been carried out on a massive scale. The remaining Serbs, most of whom are elderly persons, are being terrorised. My special envoy for the former Yugoslavia has visited the area, and I have been most distraught by his reports of what he saw." That's at the top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Move to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, top of page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, do you dispute what Ms. Ogata and her special envoy have observed and report about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this report does not in the very least contradict what I said. This report appeared in October, and I said that it was my impression that there had not been any reactions from the international community of this sort immediately after Operation Storm; rather, that they started appearing in autumn. As far as the information contained herein is concerned, I can't attest to their veracity. I can give you my opinion of them, and I have to say they -- the events, as they happened, could not in any way be construed to support the existence of a previously-devised plan. As you said, Ms. Prosecutor, this report dates from October, which is more than two months after Operation Storm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I try to avoid any further confusion. Apparently, there are three issues: The first one, whether there was burning and looting on a massive scale; the second is when the international community addressed the matter; and then the third one is whether there was a plan. I think the last question that was put to you by Mr. Waespi was whether, apart from whether you learned about it, whether you disputed that there was burning and looting on a massive scale, and Mr. Waespi, in that context, put to you this document. But let's clearly try to distinguish between the three elements in the questions as I've just said them out. I tend to agree with you, that this does not contradict anything about when you learned it, because you said this document dates from October. I see that you say, as far as whether it happened or not, you cannot confirm the veracity of this report, and although not solicited by Mr. Waespi, you added to it that you were not aware of any plan, if such things happened, that they would be the result of a plan. Let's try to clearly make a distinction between the three elements and the questions that were put to you. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ambassador, do you accept now that at one time the international community reported, and you became aware of it, that there were human rights violations on a massive scale occurring in the aftermath of Operation Storm? Do you accept that now, irrespective of the time that these reports came out?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you'll allow me to say something in order to avoid any confusion, His Honour has most helpfully distinguished between these three issues at hand here. I cannot really say to what extent the violation of human rights occurred. I cannot really tell you what the definition of the word "massive" in the context is. I can only tell you what my impression was, and this is what the Judge referred to. Secondly, at some point I did become aware of the fact that the international community raised their concerns and presented the view that human rights had been violated, in different reports, used different formulations. Again, I can't talk about the magnitude of it. I discussed the matter with all the officials of the Croatian government, and I can tell you that there were concerns about it. As for the third issue, regardless of what happened and to what extent it happened, I never had an impression that this was the result of a planned activity. It was always my opinion, and still is, that all the events, whatever happened, was the result of the lack of preparedness for what was to come after the liberation; to some extent, the lack of the preparedness, to some extent due to chance, and still others due to the situation on the ground, but definitely not as a result of an intention for things to happen that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Ambassador Galbraith, whom you started to refer to as an example of the contrary, that the international community did not report at the time you mentioned about these massive-scale violations, that's at page 18327, he testified here in this trial about the systematic destruction of the Krajina. That's at page 4960, and he said that: "This took place while the army was in control, almost from the start that the looting and burning is taking place." Do you dispute, take issue, with what Ambassador Galbraith, whom you told us yesterday you consider to be a friend, testified about?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can repeat here that I do consider Ambassador Galbraith a friend of mine and as an individual who, both as a diplomat and a politician, wanted to do good in Croatia. I cannot say that the opinion he relayed was true or untrue. From his diary, you were able to see that we were frequently in contact. I don't recall hearing such views from him in the aftermath of Operation Storm, which does not mean that I am claiming that he did not hold such views at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, he did testify that he raised these atrocities with various leaders, in particular Mr. Susak, Granic, Sarinic, and also Mr. Tudjman. You weren't aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you use a formulation such as this one, they are very general. Of course, this was a time when all manner of things were discussed with great intensity. What, precisely, these issues were is very difficult for me to pin-point. Certainly, there must be transcripts of these conversations. What I said and what I repeated today was that it was not my impression that in the several weeks following Operation Storm, the international community came up with information of, as you put it, massive-scale violation of human rights and that there was specific communication with the Croatian government on that issue. I did not have that impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. But the army, the HV, the Croatian government, they knew what was happening almost from day one. They observed, themselves, that their troops were committing crimes. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, this is something I can neither confirm nor deny. I don't know what the Croatian Army knew. What I could know and should have known from the Croatian government was the extent of the communication between the Croatian government and the international community. Of course, there was communication and there were reports. I think that the communication had to do with the following. When -- or, rather, that that communication came into play at the point when the events happening on the ground reached a level that would be cause for concern. This is what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But are you denying now that it was members of the HV, of the army, who committed some of these crimes, or do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can neither deny nor accept it. I am fully aware of the fact that I am talking about the truth as I know it, under an oath. This issue is not something I have knowledge about in order to be able to either confirm or deny it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So even today, after all these years, in your capacity as ambassador, special envoy, Geneva, New York, Washington, you still don't know that there was an admission there are documents from the HV contemporaneous at meeting that HV committed crimes like looting and burning right in the aftermath of Operation Storm? You still don't know that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor, you are putting an erroneous conclusion into my mouth. I did see the documents. I know what they state. I don't have reasons to doubt many of these documents. However, in my capacity as a witness here, I can neither confirm nor deny reports about the events on the ground which I did not observe or have any direct knowledge of. As far as reports are concerned, I did see a great many of them. And as you are well aware, they differed greatly, one from the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What differed greatly, one from the other; reports about the crimes?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. There were different reports that differed greatly in their estimation of the number of crimes, in their estimation of the incidents being isolated or organised, the estimation of various figures. There were differences in 10-fold or 50-fold figures, and I can definitely claim that there were reports that had different accounts. Again, I cannot state which of these were accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And what are these reports? Who was the author of these reports?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many informal and formal institutions producing reports. To my mind, as an ambassador and a representative of Croatia in the international community, Madam Ogata's report was very important. We also received reports from the Croatian government. We received reports from other international organisations. But, again, despite the best of my will and knowledge, I would not dare interpret these reports. Now, ten years later, more than ten years later, I recall only a few of them. You reminded me of some, but there were many, and I cannot interpret them specifically. At the time, and this is something that was not mentioned at the time, I don't recall anyone mentioning it at the time, that is to say, of the existence of a plan, and now I can tell you that there was none, but I cannot give you any sort of a qualification of the events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Ambassador. Let's move on to the next topic, and here you actually did something yesterday you professed not to do, that's talking about events that you weren't part of. That's the issue about the translation of the Croatian word "toboze", if I pronounce it correctly. Now, I accept the fact that you want to have it translated as an adjective rather than a verb, and I don't want to go into that. I just want to talk about the meaning of the word itself. Now, yesterday, while you were testifying, we made a quick search on the internet, and Your Honours, that's at 65 ter 7268, that resulted in the following proposed translations for the Croatian word "toboze." If we can get the document, please. Maybe if it could be enlarged as far as possible. Now, you see that there are all kinds of translations for the word "toboze," and I quote because it's perhaps not that well legible, "as a pretext," "would-be," "seemingly," "quasi," "professedly," "pretendedly," "ostensibly," "just for show," "smooth-faced." Now, do you accept that all these English translations are valid translations for the word "toboze"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully accept, and I am grateful for that, because it is indicative of what I wanted to draw your attention to; namely, that it's a term which is very difficult to translate into English because there isn't a term or a phrase that would clearly denote it. This is something that follows from this document of yours. However, when you translated in the way in which it was translated in the document you showed me, then it does take on a very specific meaning which, in my view, does not accurately reflect the meaning of the sentence as uttered by President Tudjman, because if you used one of the terms as proposed in the table here, you would see that it would change the meaning of the sentence. That's one matter. The other matter is where the term "toboze" was placed in the sentence. In the original, it was placed behind the verb, whereas in the translation it was placed ahead of the verb, and again it changes the meaning of the sentence in the translation, regardless of the term used to denote the original term. If you'll allow me this suggestion. If a lexical analysis were to be made of the manner of speech of President Tudjman, you would find the term "toboze" being used in his speech far more frequently than is normally the case in the Croatian language. I'm, of course, speaking this from memory, and I'm not basing it on any expertise, but if you analysed his speech you would see that -- you would see the high frequency of the use of the word "toboze" in President Tudjman's speech, next to the words -- terms such as "human rights," "freedom of press," et cetera. You would see that the way he uses this term next to, let's say, "human rights," could be, in fact, interpreted by any of these words that we have on the screen here. And there you would realise that the term "toboze" did not relate to the term "protect" in that sentence, but rather to the expression "human rights." And I do believe - or "civil rights" - and I do believe that it does make a great difference when it comes to the meaning conveyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But, Ambassador, you do accept that while we see the translation "ostensibly" here that was used yesterday by the live interpreters in the booth, and also "pretending" which is the translation we have seen in the written translation, your interpretation/translation, so-called, isn't included here? You accept that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think this is only part of the possible translations. In the waiting room for witnesses yesterday, I found an even longer list of possible translations. But my main point remains the same. That word, "toboze," however you translate it, applied to the second part of the sentence, not to the verb preceding it. That was my main objection to the written translation. You see that it's impossible to translate the word precisely, but I believe everyone now, including the Trial Chamber, can, on the basis of the proposed translations on this list, understand how broad this term is, "quasi," "seemingly," "pretendedly," because this is such a very imprecise term.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me conclude this point with a final issue. Were you aware that at the end of the sentence of President Tudjman, his comment about what you called so-called human rights, that there was a chuckle by him? Were you aware of that, or are you today aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not aware of it then. But hearing that from you now, I think it confirms what I've been saying. I knew President Tudjman very well; I worked with him a lot; and I trusted him. But I also knew that his understanding of certain concepts is not the same as the generally-accepted understanding of those concepts broadly in the world. And I'm not surprised that he chuckled when he said "human rights," because that reflects what he'd thought deep inside about this concept. However, as a responsible statement, President Tudjman, even when he did not have a deep understanding of these terms, he accepted them nevertheless because he wanted the best for Croatia. But sometimes he was prone to expressing his private reservations by using a word such as "quasi," "toboze" in Croatian, or chuckling, but of course I cannot comment on this specific situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But in this context, the chuckling about so-called human rights relates to the human rights of the Serbs living in Croatia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I'm talking about applied to the general concept that we interpret in various ways. One way is the way it is interpreted in Western democracies, and that is shared by me, personally, and by Croatia, but I don't think this applied to that specific situation. I think that if President Tudjman had been, indeed, talking about a specific plan, he would not have chuckled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, is it of any use -- I mean, as I earlier said, we have to get expert assistance here, which certainly would avoid us to look at words as "seemingly" with double "g," which does not reflect a high level of expertise. We are more or less now, as I said before, exegesis of texts. Of course, to a certain level you can do that with a witness, but let's try to avoid that witnesses here are interpreting chuckles they've not even heard. Were they loud, were they not? I mean, let's try and -- apart from that, of course, the Chamber will look at the evidence, including this sentence, in the entirety of the evidence in that context. So therefore it has become apparent now that the witness interprets the words the way in which they were expressed, chuckles added to words which he hasn't heard, in his way, whereas apparently you have a different opinion about the matter. That's -- is it of any -- I do not expect that we get the final word by putting another three or four questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I can -- I hope to have moved away from that linguistic aspect. I just wanted to have him confirm that in this context, the President Tudjman chuckled about the so-called human rights of Serbs in Croatia, not of human rights in general. That was the last point I wanted to ask the witness about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The context of the sentence, but I'm doing it now, is about them, isn't it? And I think that the Chamber would be able to read that portion in the context, whatever the witness would say about it. Of course, it's important to know from the witness what he observed as the way in which President Tudjman used words. I'm hesitant to let this go on for quite some time. So if you will have one final question on the matter, fine, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No, I'll move on to my third issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, in your witness statement, D1485, in paragraph 6 - that's on page 3 in my English version - towards the end you say that you, and I quote, "actively participated in the establishment of the ICTY." How did this come about, that you were actively participating in the establishment of the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as everyone knows here, throughout the year 1990 I played an active part in Croatian diplomacy. When the issue of establishing the Tribunal arose, as you know, the Republic of Croatia gave its support. We had a number of discussions and a number of reports made about the significance of this Tribunal, the significance of the idea. And both President Tudjman and I always supported the establishment of this Tribunal. I don't think there are any differences between those of us who were involved in diplomacy and others. Of course, Croatia considered carefully all the aspects of the possible work of this Tribunal and supported it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll come to that in a second. But before I go on, Mr. President, if the previous document, 65 ter 7268, the translation issue, could be tendered, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I guess in theory, I have no objection. I guess I question the reliability, similarly to what you pointed out, and "seemingly," isn't even spelled correctly. So I don't know the person doing this translation, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It has been shown to the witness. The witness commented on the list that was on the screen. To that extent, Mr. Waespi, the Chamber has no problems admitting it into evidence, but not as an authoritative linguistic list. As I said before, we'll have to find better sources, without spelling mistakes, to deal with the matter. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be become Exhibit P2538.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now going back to your comment about the support the Croatian Government, you, and Mr. Tudjman gave to the ICTY, that's one thing kind of supporting it, but when it came to obligations by the Croatian Government in relation to their own documents, their own alleged indictees, you obstructed the Tribunal or resisted what came from the Tribunal, did you not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. President, what is the relevance of this at this juncture? I do believe it is possibly a subject of some Rule 54 discussion, but certainly of no pertinence here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is overruled. The witness testified about the support of Croatia for the Tribunal, and I think what Mr. Waespi is doing is testing to what extent. And what he precisely will address, we'll hear from him, but he's allowed to explore this matter. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now as an ambassador, did you ever make a public statement that the Croatian Government will resist subpoenas issued by the ICTY that concerned documents related to President Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recall precisely, and I don't see exactly what you're getting at, but it's quite possible that I said, as an ambassador, that Croatia will avail itself of all legal mechanisms, but in order to present its views in this Tribunal, which does not always have to coincide with the opinion of the Prosecution. What is certain, that in all my time as a civil servant, as a minister, and as an ambassador, I always supported the work of this Tribunal, and so did the government that I participated in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, would you please focus your answer on the question. The question was not whether you always supported the work of the Tribunal. The question was whether you had given a certain statement, as far as you remember. Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Let's pull up 65 ter 7263.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: This, Mr. Ambassador, might refresh your memory about a public statement you gave -- might have given. And this is a three-page document, but the actual article by the journalist, Roy Guttman, starts in the middle of page 2, so if we could go to page -- yes, that's the right page. And if we can scroll down in the English version. Yes. That's a clip from an organisation, news organisation called "Newsday," and it mentions you, Mr. Zuzul, Miomir Zuzul, as the Croatian ambassador to the US, talking about arresting war criminals in Bosnia. And then on page 3 there is the following quote: "The Croatian envoy also said his government will resist subpoenas handed down by the Tribunal for internal documents connecting Tudjman and his aids with the war waged in Bosnia by Bosnian Croats." So that was the extent of your support towards the ICTY and the international community in this regard. Do you remember that quote?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you've just done what the Presiding Judge had cautioned me against. You first made a conclusion and then asked the question, and the conclusion is wrong. You can find thousands of documents confirming that I always cooperated with the Tribunal as the representative of the Croatian government, even when that was difficult. This sentence, the way it is phrased, you can see that it's a report from a briefing at the embassy. It could have been interpreted and written in any which way, but it meant only this: If Croatia were to resist, it would resist with full respect for this Tribunal. And where will it resist? Before the Court. In the 1990s, you will remember, Croatia did react to certain subpoenas, and that is a right that Croatia had. It certainly does not mean contempt of the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'd like to tender --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, first -- I'll give you an opportunity, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I recently heard you saying, "I don't know what you're getting at." Let Mr. Waespi consider what he's getting at. Second, you're saying, "You're doing exactly what the Presiding Judge said I should not do." There is a difference between the way in which questions are phrased, whether conclusions are put to you, and the question is, "Is that conclusion right, isn't that the case," that's different from answers to be given by a witness. So therefore I would invite you to refrain from commenting on the questions. Or if there's any problem with the way in which Mr. Waespi formulates his questions, the Chamber either will proprio motu comment on it or the other party, and that might happen now, I don't know. But Mr. Kehoe is on his feet; Mr. Kehoe is certainly able to object to any question which is not put in a form which is appropriate and acceptable in this court. Mr. Kehoe, I don't know whether you had this in mind or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I did, Mr. President, and my brief comment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Demonstrates that immediately, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: My brief comment of course is the good-faith basis for this, because I'm sure that the Office of the Prosecutor knows full well, and the Court of course can take judicial notice of decisions of the Appellate Chamber, that this particular issue was litigated two months later and the Republic of Croatia prevailed on this particular issue concerning subpoenas to the Republic of Croatia concerning the war with the Bosnian Croats. So I do believe the good-faith basis will require a full picture of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although I think that, as it appears already from the answer of the witness, that where the question is formulated with certain limitations, that the witness apparently is fully capable of putting matters in context in this respect. But thank you for -- you're supposed not to comment on questions, but nevertheless I do understand that your objection is that it's phrased in such a way that it may mislead. Mr. Waespi, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just an issue in the transcript. On the previous page, page 28, line 18, you said, Mr. Ambassador, at least it's transcribed as such, that in the 1990s you will remember Croatia did react to certain subpoenas and that it's a right that Croatia had. Did you say that or did you say "did not react to certain subpoenas"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, yes, Croatia did react. That's what I said. I said it seems to me that towards the end of the 1990s, Croatia did react, but it reacted before this Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to understand. Did you intend to say -- because you added to that "that is a right that Croatia had." Now, if you follow an order contained in the subpoena, you usually would not say, That's a right we had, but it's, rather, an obligation. Did you want to say that Croatia responded to subpoenas and that there was some dispute about it, because I have difficulties in understanding the -- following the subpoena, reacting to it. Reaction could be positive, could be negative, so therefore the word "reaction" is not unambiguous, especially since it's followed by the words, and it had a right to do so, that I got the impression, but please correct me when I'm wrong, that there was some kind of a challenge in whether this subpoena was issued in accordance with, well, let's say existing international law or whatever, because of course the Chamber is aware that there has been quite a dispute about what - especially when state security interests are concerned - what subpoenas -- where a status under an obligation to, without any reservation, follow an order contained in the subpoenas and where it is not. That has been litigated in quite some detail. Is that what you wanted to refer to or -- the word "reaction" is not unambiguous. That's my problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my recollection, and I think you are completely correct, these are two completely different meanings. The way I understood it, and it may not be the only possible understanding, the way I understood the question of the Prosecution, it related to a question, What would happen with the announced subpoenas, or subpoenas that the Prosecution had already moved for, concerning the Republic of Croatia? The position of the government was that they would address the competent Trial Chamber and move that such subpoenas not be issued, and that's what I think happened. The Republic of Croatia exercised its legal right to react to the position of the Prosecution. Now, when I think back, I think that was the discussion and that was the legal right concerned. If the Trial Chamber had issued the subpoena in question, I don't think a single Croatian government has so far challenged a subpoena issued by a Trial Chamber. And in every government that I participated in, every time cooperation was sought from us, we cooperated, without any subpoenas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, because you earlier said at page 28, lines 15 and 16, that, you know, this was a press briefing and it could be interpreted or written in any which way, did you say at that briefing, if you remember after such a long time, words to the effect that the Croatian government, and I quote from this article, "will resist subpoenas handed down by the Tribunal for internal documents connecting Tudjman and his aids with the war waged in Bosnia by Bosnian Croats"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way the Presiding Judge interpreted it, I would never utter such a sentence expressing resistance to the Tribunal. If I said anything like it, I only meant the right of the Croatia to challenge a subpoena before the Court, I repeat, before the Court. But after a final decision had been rendered by a Trial Chamber, I would never have said that Croatia should ignore or resist such a decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Do you know Journalist Roy Guttman?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: What's his reputation?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: His reputation is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I'd like to tender this document, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm somewhat perplexed, given where we're going with this. Number 1, none of this is in quotes. But, more importantly, just going back to my foundation to the effect that this was, in fact, litigated and the OTP lost in front of the Appellate Chamber. I don't -- I'm concerned that the OTP is attempting to use this for a point that the actual facts mitigate directly against, and that is that it was litigated, consistent with what the witness said, and the OTP lost?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the litigation was quite complex, but let me ask you a question, Mr. Zuzul. Apart from how we should interpret your words, does this article reflect what you said, or perhaps not in your exact own wording, but does it more or less reflect what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, now glancing through the article, I think the answer is "yes," but I think in this passage, which is just a small passage in the article concerning the support that Croatia would give to the arrest of war criminals, we see that the tone of the whole article is quite different. And there are no quotation marks, so none of these are direct quotations. I certainly did not say something like this, the way the Prosecutor is trying to interpret it. It sounds completely different from anything I said. And despite all my appreciation of Roy Guttman, I cannot accept that this is, indeed, a sentence I uttered, the way it is interpreted here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document will be MFI'd. The Chamber will consider whether or not to admit it into evidence. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will become Exhibit P2539, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'd like to turn to my last topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I look at the clock and see that it's 10.30. Mr. Waespi, how much time would you need for your last topic?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we would need to have a break first. We'll have a break, and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Before I start again, I want to report that we have no objections to these video-clips that are connected with Mr. Galbraith. Actually, Mr. Tieger told me last night, and I forgot.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, in your dealings with the international community, you were presented with a lot of concerns about the return of the Krajina Serbs; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And there are instances, at least one of them, that you tried to shrug off these inquiries; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure that I understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That when members of the international community told you that the Krajina Serbs should return, that you said, No, that's not an issue, and you tried to divert their attention to other issues that are less painful for you?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you are faced with complex issues, and in diplomacy all issues are complex, of course you will always try to place the emphasis or draw the attention to matters that are favourable to you. I did not have such discussions where I would say that this was not an issue or that it should not be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's look at one of these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, this is 65 ter 7261. And I'd like to go to page 5 in English and page 12 in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ambassador, this is a meeting at the Presidential Palace on 9 September, 9 September 1995, and if we go to page 5 we will see a reference by you to a Mr. Tarnoff. And I think we have heard about him yesterday. Can you, if you recall, remind us who Mr. Tarnoff was?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that at the time Mr. Tarnoff was under-secretary of state. Unless I'm mistaken, he was under-secretary of state for political issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And that's an American diplomat, then?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: An American diplomat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me quote what you said in this meeting, and the president, Tudjman, is present, Mr. Granic as well, and others: "Miomir Zuzul: President, in connection with this Tarnoff, as the minister was having lunch with the French, I had a chance to spend some time with Tarnoff alone. He began. First he mentioned the problem of Krajina Serbs. I replied swiftly that we have a lot more important issues than this one, so that he did not insist on it." Isn't that an example to show that the issue of Krajina Serbs was clearly something you didn't want to talk about and didn't want to deal with?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that this indicates precisely what I said. I believe that we had many issues that we had to discuss with the United States of America, and I wanted to make use of the opportunity to talk to Mr. Tarnoff on these matters as best I could. I did not evade, nor could I have evaded, as a diplomat, the issue of the problems faced by the Krajina Serbs. Oftentimes, the information or the instructions I had did not allow me to engage in specific talks, which does not go to say that I evaded such talks. But in my discussions with such a high-level representative of the US, I wanted to discuss matters that were of paramount importance to me, which had mostly to do with the issue of the peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Following up on a comment you just made, did you receive instructions from your government not to engage in specific talks about the return of the Krajina Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received such instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So what were the instructions that you received or you mentioned that did not allow you to engage in talks? What were you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how it was interpreted to you, but I said that I never received instructions that would not allow me something. However, as with any job, likewise in diplomacy and in our relations with the international community, we said we had a certain hierarchy which was that of the importance in our communication with the international community. I said that there were more important matters that needed to be discussed with the United States of America. This is what I referred to, and I believe that Mr. Tarnoff accepted this. Had he insisted on his point, I would not have refused to give him an answer. In the State Department and elsewhere, I discussed many problematic issue, which was only a normal thing to do in the relations between two states.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be become Exhibit P2540.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Ambassador, it is also correct, isn't it, that you told a fellow ambassador that he should, quote, "forget about the return of the Krajina Serbs, the return would only cause trouble"?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way it is quoted here, I categorically state that it is not an accurate representation, the way it is quoted here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let's go to P458. That's an exhibit you have been presented with by Mr. Kehoe yesterday, diplomatic diary of Ambassador Galbraith. And the quote I'm referring to is on page 38, in e-court, and the diary itself has a specific separate number, which is page 44. And you see on the previous page that it's an entry of September 5, so let's see what Ambassador Galbraith talks about in his diary. The top of this page: "I had dinner with some ambassadors (Russia, Spain, Canada), and DCMs (UK, Germany, France), to discuss the situation. I was disturbed when Zuzul, whom I consider a moderate and decent man, told me on Saturday to forget about the return of the Krajina Serbs. 'Their return would only cause trouble,' he said." Do you accept what Ambassador Galbraith wrote in his diary?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, of course, do accept that he wrote it, but I do not accept that I said it and that it is a quotation of what I said. Mr. Galbraith and I had many discussions on various issues, as you can see from his diary. It may have been a conclusion that he arrived at on the basis of a conversation which I do not remember at all. I don't remember either the conversation or the sentence, but I cannot accept that this is the sort of sentence that I would utter. I discussed with him and others all the difficulties in the way of the return. As a diplomat, as an intellectual, and as a psychologist, I was and am still aware of all these problems. However, I would not have uttered a sentence which would have implied that there should be no return. I definitely did not say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Ambassador, there is evidence in this case that members of the Croatian leadership publicly called the Serbs a cancer in Croatia. Do you agree with such language?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd like to go to 65 ter 7259, and this is a "New York Times" article dated 15 July 1995. Perhaps we can go to page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: In the first few paragraphs, there are comments made by Mr. Martic talking about retaliation against Croatian cities, and then a comment by a Croatia citizen, Vera Golubic, who supports an attack against the Krajina Serbs, despite Martic's threats against the cities because, as she says, "it's better than being hostage to the Serbs for years and years." And then the article goes on as follows: "Croatian envoy at the UN in Geneva, Miomir Zuzul, took a similar position in an interview broadcast on Zagreb TV this week." "'We have a cancer in our body,' Mr. Zuzul said. 'When you have such a disease, you cannot wait forever.'" Ambassador, you clearly adopt the language that Mr. Tudjman and others publicly used; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Prosecutor. First of all, this is a quotation of a quotation, because it is reported here that I stated this in another interview and not this one. That's number one. Number two, where do you, in this sentence of mine, see any reference to Serbs? I don't see any. If I did say something like this, if I did, which is possible, it has a meaning which is quite different from the one you want to allude to. I am not referring to Serbs. This has never been my position, and this has never been the sort of language I would use in reference to another nation. I am referring to the fact that a part of Croatia was occupied, and that's the truth. This was the disease in the Croatian body that could not be sustained as a state of affairs. But I did not imply here, not by a far shot, that some other nation would be the cancer on one's body, not in any way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will become Exhibit P2541.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zuzul, before I give an opportunity to Mr. Kehoe to put more questions to you, I have one very specific question. Questioned by the Court:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier today, Mr. Waespi asked you about your testimony yesterday, about that you did not receive information which would allude to any massive violation of human rights. You said quite the contrary, there was an intervention on the part of Ambassador Galbraith when he joined a group of departing Serbs, possibly in an attempt to prevent any adverse effects it may have. And then you said: "I invited Ambassador Galbraith, and he was accompanied by an entire high-level US delegation to the place where I grew up to attend a large public event. My intention was for him to simply see what sort of reaction the simple folk would have upon seeing him and the American delegation, and that nobody would perceive his calls for the protection of the civilians in a negative way." Quite a simple question: Where did you take him? What is the place where you grew up?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took him to Imotski. It's a place in Dalmatinska Zagora, where, on the 15th of August, a religious festivity is traditionally celebrated, which is that of The Lady of Nativity, or, rather, The Nativity of Our Lady, and it always attracts a large crowd of people. Let me explain to you why was it that I invited him. We were friends. There were negative reports in the Croatian media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you would first give me more specific information, where to find that place exactly on the map, so that I know where it is, approximately. If you take one of the cities and then to tell me to go south, or north, or west, or east, then I'll -- apparently it's on the Dalmatian coast. Could you tell us where?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the town itself is not located on the coast. It's between the coast and the Mount Biokovo on the stretch from Split to Mostar, by the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina, but in Croatia. It's a small town. You can find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, maybe I can help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: If you go south of Split, you find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just find -- I want to be quite clear to you. I'm using Google Maps at this moment to see where. Okay, go south from Split ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: To a town called Makarska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I've got that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: And then if you go north straight up, it's roughly in that area. Imotski, it's on the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I see it, yes. Just for my information, was there -- I'm trying to -- I do understand why you took Mr. Galbraith there. Was that an area where there had been combat recently or ...

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not an area where fighting took place, but it was an area from where great numbers of volunteers who joined the Croatian Army hailed. It was an area of Croatia that was marked by the fact that it was not directly affected by the war, but it had nevertheless given most of the men who were subsequently killed as members of the Croatian Army. I think that more than 100 men from that town were killed in the war. The festivity involved was one that is held very dearly in religious terms, but it is also an area that is characterized by strong national sentiments. It is a matter that was proved through history. In that area, before the war, during the war, and following the war, a certain number of ethnic Serbs lived as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, you gave this answer when you were questioned about looting and burning and whether that took place on a massive scale, and what concerns you had, and what you learned from the internationals. I have difficulties in fully understanding how this would shed light on the matters that were asked, because apparently this was a place where no combat had taken place. May I take it that there was no burning or looting in that area you observed when going there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that an area dominantly populated by Croats or Serbs, or would it differ from one village to another?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation varies from village to village. Both Croats and Serbs lived there. Let us say the village adjacent to the one where festivities took place has the majority Serb population, and I do know that they do still live there. Nobody tried to drive them out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it may be the case that I was giving my answer in a different context because, in my view, what I referred to did not have to do with mass-scale burning or expulsion, it was driving at something else, and perhaps the context then made it unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How did you travel to this place, from where, because you said you took him there?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was waiting for him there. I was already there. He arrived that morning with the entire delegation from Split.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From Split. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Kehoe, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I could just follow up on what you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, of course, you are free to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, as usual, just taking the lead from the President's questions, can you explain to us again, why did you bring Ambassador Galbraith, and I think you noted it was Ambassador Holbrooke as well and General Clark, I believe were the others, and correct me if I'm wrong, why did you bring them to Imotski on Ascension Day on the 15th of August?

utterances.speaker: MIOMIR ZUZUL [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ambassador Galbraith, a few days before that when a group of Serbs from Croatia was moving, leaving Croatia, and carrying their belongings on tractors, joined this group. Ambassador Galbraith joined this group. Some Croatian media criticised him and attacked him because of this, because that was the time just after the military victory, and there was a tendency among certain individuals, certain journalists, to express different views. I did not want Ambassador Galbraith, or Americans, or the international community to get the impression that normal Croatian people, ordinary Croatian people, see anything wrong with what Ambassador Galbraith had done. I believe that he, himself, was rather nervous because he wasn't sure what to expect of this normal Croatian crowd. I even asked him to come to this improvised alter where about 20.000 to 25.000 Croats had come to celebrate a religious holiday and to see for himself how these normal Croatian people, who were not coached by anyone, who were not instructed by anyone, would react to him and how they would receive him. And as he writes in his diary, he was greeted by an ovation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. I have no further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there -- may I take it that the Cermak and Markac Defence still have no questions for the witness? Which means, Mr. Zuzul -- and please forgive me for not calling you "Ambassador." It's my habit for whoever comes here, whether it's a military authority, whether it's a diplomatic authority, just to address them as "Mr.," and so on, in that respect. I treat everyone in the same way, including Mr. Galbraith. This concludes your testimony in this courtroom. We'd like to thank you very much for coming to The Hague and to answer all the questions put to you by the parties and by the Bench. And I wish you -- although you never know whether a diplomat then travels home, but finally I wish you a safe trip home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please escort Mr. Zuzul out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe or Mr. Misetic. Mr. Misetic, are you ready to call your next witness? And we will first deal with protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we start to turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, Wednesday, the 10th of June, 9.00, Courtroom III. And for everyone who wants to attend, there's a great likelihood that we would immediately turn into closed session again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 10th day of June, 2009, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
